title: The First Waves of Amphibious Assault Will Be Unmanned
gist: Brian Kerg argues that the precision-strike regime has made manned opposed amphibious assault operationally and politically infeasible — the last brigade-scale opposed landing was Sri Lanka's Operation Balavegaya in 1991 — but Ukraine's July 13, 2026 fully uncrewed amphibious assault (an uncrewed boat landing an armed unmanned ground vehicle) reopens the mission by transferring first-wave risk to robots. He predicts brigade-equivalent unmanned landings within one to two years and calls on the Marine Corps to pull forward the 2040–2045 time horizon in its 21st Century Concept for Amphibious Operations.

themes.theme: Precision-Strike Regime Killed the Manned Landing

insights.claim: In the precision-strike regime, where surveillance is ubiquitous and long-range strike can be massed cheaply and at scale, the likelihood of a large-scale opposed amphibious operation succeeding is increasingly bleak.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: Undercuts the investment case for large-deck amphibious platforms and favors cheap, attritable maritime systems.
insights.quote: an enemy that can see and strike the amphibious force is one that will not face an amphibious assault
insights.locator: In the wake of the precision-strike regime

insights.claim: The attacking amphibious force must defend successfully against every strike while the defender needs to be right or lucky only once to sink a ship carrying thousands of troops and render the landing infeasible.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: Classic asymmetric-defense math that also governs carrier and tanker risk pricing in contested littorals.
insights.quote: But the defender only needs to be right or lucky only once to send an amphibious ship full of thousands of troops into the briny deep

insights.claim: The defender's advantage peaks during the first waves of an assault because the task force is pinned to the operating area, the assault force cannot fight while moving ship-to-shore, and the first troops ashore are disorganized and unconsolidated.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: Identifies the precise phase where unmanned substitution buys the most risk reduction — the target market for robotic landing craft.
insights.locator: The defender's advantage is at its zenith

insights.claim: The last known major opposed amphibious assault — at least brigade-sized against a significantly defended area — was the Sri Lankan Armed Forces' Operation Balavegaya in 1991, and it succeeded only because the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam had no anti-ship weapons.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: A 35-year drought is the hardest empirical evidence that the mission set is obsolete in its manned form.
insights.locator: The last known major opposed amphibious assault on record

insights.claim: Modern opposed amphibious landings only occur when defenders lack substantial anti-ship weapons and the attacker so overwhelmingly outmatches them that resistance is token.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: Anti-ship missile proliferation is the single variable that decides whether a coastline is assaultable.
insights.locator: When modern opposed amphibious landings occur

insights.claim: The Allies shelved Operation Causeway, the planned attack on Japanese-occupied Taiwan, largely because Taiwan's geography alone gave defenders too much advantage.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: Taiwan's terrain has deterred amphibious planners since 1944 — a durable input to cross-strait invasion probability estimates.
insights.locator: The Allies shelved Operation Causeway

insights.claim: The Falklands War was the transition point where amphibious operational risk became gravely apparent: Argentinian forces stopped attacking the British task force not because of British action but because they ran out of Exocet missiles.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: Magazine depth, not defensive skill, determined the outcome — an argument for judging modern threats by munition inventories.
insights.quote: Argentinian forces did not stop shooting because of British actions, but only because they ran out of Exocet missiles.

insights.claim: Gen. Norman Schwarzkopf scrapped the plan to liberate Kuwait City with two Marine expeditionary brigades in an amphibious assault, largely because of Iraqi naval mining of the Persian Gulf and Iraqi anti-ship missiles including the Exocet.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: Sea mines — cheap and old — have cancelled a two-brigade landing once and remain the lowest-cost area-denial tool.
insights.locator: Gen. Norman Schwarzkopf famously scrapped plans

insights.claim: Russia massed landing ships in the Black Sea for an amphibious assault on Odesa in the opening weeks of the 2022 invasion, but abandoned it after Ukraine sank the flagship Moskva with Neptune missiles and struck other landing ships.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: A live demonstration that a handful of shore-launched missiles can void an entire amphibious campaign.

insights.claim: Despite the most massive and rapid naval buildup in history and constant regional aggression, China has not attempted an amphibious assault on Taiwanese territory since 1955.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: Naval tonnage alone has not translated into demonstrated amphibious willingness — a caution against reading PLAN shipbuilding as invasion timing.

insights.claim: Talks of an amphibious assault on Kharg Island have arisen during the ongoing war between the United States and Iran but have gone nowhere.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: Kharg is Iran's main crude export terminal; a seizure attempt would be a step-change in oil risk premium — and the author signals it is not happening.

insights.claim: Ukraine, without a navy, rendered the Russian Black Sea Fleet rudderless, demonstrating that shore-based and unmanned systems can defeat a conventional fleet.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: The cost-exchange ratio favors sea denial over sea control — a structural headwind for large surface combatant programs.

insights.claim: Despite Operation Rough Rider, the March 2025 U.S. punishment campaign, the Houthis can still strike nearly at will within the Red Sea.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: Persistent Red Sea interdiction risk means elevated shipping insurance and Suez rerouting stay structural, not episodic.

insights.claim: Iran, despite sustained and withering strikes from the United States and Israel, can still deny access to the Strait of Hormuz.

themes.theme: Ukraine's Uncrewed Landing as Inflection Point

insights.claim: On July 13, 2026, the Ukrainian military released video of the first completely unmanned amphibious assault: an uncrewed amphibious boat landed on a beach, dropped its ramp, and released an unmanned ground vehicle that moved ashore and opened fire by remote-control machine gun.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: The proof-of-concept event that starts the clock on a new procurement category — robotic landing craft and armed UGVs.
insights.quote: An uncrewed amphibious boat landed at a beach, dropped its ramp, and released an unmanned ground vehicle which moved ashore and opened fire by remote-control machine gun.
insights.locator: On July 13, 2026, the Ukrainian military released a video

insights.claim: Within one or two years, unmanned amphibious operations could scale to forces analogous to a manned brigade or larger, because a fully mobilized modern nation can adapt at scale faster than ever.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: A concrete 2027–2028 milestone to test; if it happens, amphibious deterrence assumptions for Taiwan and the Baltics need repricing.
insights.quote: It is reasonable to expect that within one or two years, such operations could occur, consisting of forces analogous to a manned brigade or larger.
insights.locator: But adaptation at scale by a modern nation

insights.claim: Even devastating losses to a defending force become tolerable when the attacker can reproduce unmanned equipment far faster than traditional amphibious capabilities and without the political cost of losing thousands of lives.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: Shifts the binding constraint from casualty tolerance to factory throughput — favoring producers of attritable platforms.

insights.claim: As with most technological leaps in warfare, the first instance looks trivially small — Ukraine's demonstration involved a single boat and a single ground vehicle, 'a far cry from a fully uncrewed Normandy.'
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: A reminder to price early, small-scale military demos as options rather than dismissing them as stunts.

themes.theme: Escalation Asymmetry Between Drones and Humans

insights.claim: Losing unmanned assets does not trigger the escalation spiral that losing crewed platforms does: Iran's June 2019 shootdown of a U.S. Navy RQ-4A Global Hawk over the Strait of Hormuz nearly produced retaliatory strikes that were ultimately called off and tensions cooled rapidly.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: Drone losses are a low-escalation signaling channel; markets should discount headline drone incidents relative to manned losses.

insights.claim: After Iranian forces shot down a U.S. F-15E Strike Eagle over Iran in April 2026 during Operation Epic Fury, massive retaliatory strikes and escalation threats followed alongside a combat search and rescue mission that itself cost aircraft.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: The contrast case: crewed losses reliably escalate, which is the political mechanism unmanned first waves are designed to bypass.

insights.claim: Losing a single major amphibious ship forces the attacking country's executive into a dilemma between embarrassing withdrawal and massive escalation, so savvy leaders avoid selecting opposed amphibious assaults at all.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: Explains why high-casualty options get pre-emptively removed from menus — a filter for forecasting which military actions actually occur.

themes.theme: Cost Structure of Robotic Landing Craft

insights.claim: Landing craft built for a robotic landing force are cheaper and faster to manufacture than traditional L-class ships because they shed life-support systems and the force protection needed to guard human cargo.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: Removing human accommodation is the cost lever that makes a numerous, attritable amphibious fleet economically possible.
insights.locator: Moreover, landing craft built specifically for a robotic landing force

insights.claim: The high cost of manning, training, and equipping ship's companies incentivizes navies to build relatively few large amphibious ships rather than a massive fleet of smaller ones that would complicate an enemy's targeting dilemma.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: Personnel economics — not naval architecture — is why fleets are concentrated and therefore targetable.
insights.locator: This cost, compounded by the investment in manning

insights.claim: The rate at which Ukraine replaces the drones it expends daily against Russia offers a useful benchmark for how quickly and cheaply combat losses of unmanned amphibious systems could be replaced.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: Ukrainian drone attrition-replacement rates become the reference metric for pricing attritable naval programs.

insights.claim: The Marine Corps moved away from opposed forcible entry at scale after 2020 precisely because of the precision-strike regime, favoring expeditionary advanced bases and stand-in forces — so recalibrating again toward unmanned assault would look like an abrupt and unsupportable U-turn.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: Institutional sunk cost, not technology, is the main obstacle to a US unmanned amphibious program.
insights.locator: Such a shift raises key questions for the Force Design initiative

insights.claim: The Marine Corps Warfighting Lab's unclassified 21st Century Concept for Amphibious Operations anticipates seizure of key maritime terrain, penetration of contested areas, and proliferation of unmanned systems, but on a 2040–2045 horizon set before Ukraine's uncrewed demonstration.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: The doctrinal timeline is roughly 15 years behind observed reality — a case for accelerated unmanned maritime budgets.

insights.claim: Because the United States is not presently under acute military pressure and faces a fiscally restrained environment with soaring competing technology demands, it may be too slow to develop unmanned amphibious capability.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: Budget crowding among tech modernization lines means winners will be few — watch which programs get line-item protection.

insights.claim: Amphibious operations remain a core competency, crown jewel, and legal mandate for the Marine Corps, which keeps a line of thought alive inside the service that assault in some form remains a future capability.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: Statutory mandate means the mission will not be abandoned outright — it will be re-equipped, creating a procurement opening.

insights.claim: It is unproven whether an uncrewed landing force can do more than establish initial combat power ashore — stabilizing and expanding the lodgment or breaking out to seize ports, airfields, and crossroads remains a technological aspiration no one has demonstrated.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: Caps near-term expectations: robotic first waves are an enabler, not a replacement for ground forces.

insights.claim: Follow-on waves beyond the first will almost certainly require human formations both to bring other elements of combat power and to maintain and repair the unmanned systems to keep them in the fight.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: Field maintenance and sustainment of robotic fleets becomes a distinct and underrated capability requirement.

insights.claim: Defenders can deploy drones at scale to neutralize an uncrewed attacking force at sea or on the beach, turning the engagement into a contest of mass, attrition, production capacity, and replacement speed.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: Robot-versus-robot warfare makes industrial throughput the decisive military variable — an argument for manufacturing capacity as a strategic asset.
insights.quote: If two such opposing robotic forces collide, the contest will become one of mass, attrition, production capacity, and replacement speed.

insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: Reframes amphibious deterrence as a manufacturing-capacity race, which advantages China's shipbuilding scale.

insights.claim: Amphibious assaults retain unique strategic value because they bypass massed forces and strong points, insert ground forces into the enemy rear, and create sudden campaign momentum — which is why the capability is worth rebuilding rather than retiring.
insights.speaker: Brian Kerg
insights.so_what: The demand-side case: preserving amphibious options widens a state's foreign-policy latitude, sustaining program funding.
insights.locator: Despite their enormous risks, amphibious assaults offer critical options
